query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for plasma-facing applications in fusion reactors, what single intervention could improve radiation tolerance while preserving mechanical integrity and engineering practicality? Formulate one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the proposed mechanism, predicts a measurable improvement over the unmodified baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites prior evidence supporting the causal rationale, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor fraction (~5 at.%) of a refractory dopant (such as Mo) to a baseline equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its radiation tolerance under fusion plasma-facing conditions by promoting localized defect recombination without compromising its mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory HEA with established high strength, hardness, and thermal stability.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at.% of a dopant element (e.g., Mo) into the TaNbHfZr alloy to increase compositional complexity.
generation.conditions: Irradiation at fusion-relevant conditions, for example under helium ion or heavy ion exposure at elevated temperatures (773–973 K) and irradiation doses representative of plasma-facing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local lattice distortion and modified defect migration landscape induced by the additional element.
generation.mechanism: The dopant increases compositional complexity and local lattice strain, which reduces the mean free path of point defects and encourages their localized recombination rather than clustering into voids or large defect structures. This mechanism—analogous to effects observed in Ni-based SP-CSAs—should reduce defect cluster size and void swelling while maintaining the alloy’s overall mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline TaNbHfZr alloy, the doped alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable reduction in defect cluster size (potentially approaching an order-of-magnitude reduction in cluster dimensions) and decreased void swelling, while preserving similar yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Unmodified equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory HEA under the same irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the dopant concentration remains low (e.g., around 5 at.%), as higher additions may lead to undesirable phase segregation or a deterioration of mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact dopant concentration, choice of dopant element (using Mo here as an example), and precise quantitative improvements in defect metrics remain to be established experimentally. Moreover, transferring the mechanism observed in Ni-based alloys to refractory HEAs carries some uncertainty that must be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline equimolar TaNbHfZr alloy and another set with ~5 at.% Mo added. Subject both sets to identical irradiation experiments under fusion-relevant conditions (e.g., helium ion irradiation at 773–973 K, reaching similar doses). Post-irradiation, perform microstructural analysis using TEM and other methods and assess mechanical properties via yield strength and ductility measurements.
measurements: Defect cluster size distribution and void densities via TEM
Quantitative void swelling analysis (e.g., using X-ray diffraction or volumetric measurements)
Mechanical property evaluations (yield strength, ductility) from stress-strain testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in defect cluster size or void swelling compared to the baseline, or if there is a measurable degradation in its mechanical properties beyond acceptable ranges, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The HEAs are also resistant to forming large defect clusters compared with binary nickel alloy systems and have the self-healing effect. Dislocation loops and lines can significantly affect the hardening and embrittlement, but in CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi, the density of dislocation loops after irradiation by Ni ions was higher than that of binary and ternary nickel alloys, and most of these loops had a smaller size []. The reasons for the self-healing of HEAs include high atomic stress and lattice distortion caused by the large difference in atomic size, which lead to the amorphization followed by crystallization of the alloy [,], and the similarity of vacancy and interstitial migration energies, which improve the defect annihilation []. Thus, the structural features of the HEAs affect the radiation resistance.

The integrated experimental and modelling work shows that reduced defect mobility and altered migration paths on a modified energy landscape, resulting from alloy complexity, can modify defect dynamics to promote annihilation of radiation damage that ultimately enhance radiation tolerance. Irradiation-induced void formation in nickel and Ni-containing equiatomic SP-CSAs at elevated temperature is controlled by the migration behaviours of interstitial clusters. Short-range 3D motion of interstitial clusters that significantly increases the vacancy–interstitial recombination rate plays a key role in preventing significant void swelling in NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn. The mechanism has been revealed by TEM observation and confirmed by MD simulation. Composition complexity and lattice distortion due to the alloy components effectively modify the defect migration behaviour in the equiatomic SP-CSAs. More localized migration of interstitial clusters enhances recombination of point defects in the cascade region where the defects are created. reading.lever: Tuning compositional complexity by controlled elemental additions to boost localized defect recombination.
reading.why: Prior evidence in Ni-based SP-CSAs shows that increased alloy complexity reduces defect clustering, a mechanism likely transferable to refractory HEAs.
